title: IMCI general danger signs (under-5)
text: A child with any general danger sign needs urgent referral: unable to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions (current or during this illness), lethargic or unconscious. Assess every sick child for these before anything else.
source: WHO Integrated Management of Childhood Illness — Chart booklet
section: IMCI general danger signs

title: Fast-breathing thresholds for childhood pneumonia
text: Count breaths for one minute. Fast breathing = 50 or more breaths/min for an infant 2-11 months, and 40 or more breaths/min for a child 12 months up to 5 years. Fast breathing or chest indrawing indicates pneumonia and warrants antibiotics.
source: WHO Integrated Management of Childhood Illness — Chart booklet
section: IMCI cough or difficult breathing

title: ORS + zinc for childhood diarrhoea
text: Treat diarrhoea with low-osmolarity oral rehydration solution (ORS) plus zinc for 10-14 days: 20 mg/day for children, 10 mg/day for infants under 6 months. Zinc reduces the duration and severity of the episode and the likelihood of recurrence over the following 2-3 months.
source: Clinical management of acute diarrhoea: WHO/UNICEF joint statement (WHO/FCH/CAH/04.7)
section: WHO/UNICEF Acute Diarrhoea Management

title: Metformin for type 2 diabetes
text: Metformin is the first-line oral medicine for type 2 diabetes in adults and is on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines. Typical adult dosing starts at 500 mg once or twice daily with meals and is titrated up; it is contraindicated in significant renal impairment.
source: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, 23rd list
section: WHO EML Section 18.5 — Insulins and other medicines used for diabetes

title: Amoxicillin for non-severe childhood pneumonia
text: Oral amoxicillin is first-line for non-severe (fast-breathing) pneumonia in children, having replaced oral cotrimoxazole. Refer urgently if there are general danger signs or chest indrawing with severe features.
source: Revised WHO classification and treatment of childhood pneumonia at health facilities
section: WHO Childhood Pneumonia Revision 2014

title: Hypertension diagnostic threshold
text: Hypertension is generally diagnosed when office systolic blood pressure is 140 mmHg or higher, or diastolic is 90 mmHg or higher, on more than one occasion. Confirm with repeat measurements; isolated elevated readings are not sufficient.
source: WHO Guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults
section: WHO Hypertension 2021 Section 3.1

title: Preferred first-line ART (dolutegravir-based)
text: WHO's preferred first-line antiretroviral therapy for adults is a dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimen, typically tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir (the single-pill TLD). Dolutegravir is preferred for both first- and second-line for its efficacy, tolerability, and high genetic barrier to resistance.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 4.3 — First-line ART regimens

title: Stavudine (d4T) is no longer recommended
text: Stavudine (d4T)-based regimens are no longer recommended. WHO advised phasing out stavudine because of frequent, often irreversible mitochondrial toxicity — peripheral neuropathy, lipoatrophy, and lactic acidosis; tenofovir (TDF) or zidovudine (AZT) are the recommended nucleoside backbones instead.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 4.3 — Discontinuation of stavudine

title: Treat-all: start ART regardless of CD4
text: WHO recommends antiretroviral therapy for everyone diagnosed with HIV, regardless of CD4 count or WHO clinical stage ('treat all'), and as early as possible after diagnosis.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 4.1 — When to start ART

title: WHO clinical staging of HIV
text: WHO clinical staging grades HIV disease severity from stage 1 (asymptomatic) through stage 2 (mild symptoms), stage 3 (advanced — e.g. significant weight loss, persistent fever or diarrhoea, pulmonary TB) to stage 4 (severe / AIDS-defining illness). It is used alongside CD4 to guide management.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 3 — Clinical staging

title: Role of the CD4 count
text: The CD4 count reflects immune status in HIV; lower counts mean higher risk of opportunistic infection. A CD4 below 200 cells/mm3 indicates advanced HIV disease and the need for opportunistic-infection prophylaxis. ART is started regardless of the CD4 count.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 5.1 — Advanced HIV disease

title: ART adherence
text: Sustained high adherence to antiretroviral therapy is essential to achieve and maintain viral suppression and to prevent drug resistance; adherence assessment and support are part of routine HIV care at every visit.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 6 — Service delivery and adherence

title: TB in people living with HIV
text: Tuberculosis is the leading cause of death among people living with HIV. WHO recommends routine TB symptom screening at every visit and TB preventive treatment (e.g. isoniazid preventive therapy) for people with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 5.4 — TB/HIV co-infection

title: Co-trimoxazole preventive therapy
text: Co-trimoxazole preventive therapy is recommended for people living with HIV who have advanced disease or a low CD4 count, to prevent Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) and other opportunistic infections.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 5.2 — Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis

title: The CIEL concept dictionary
text: The CIEL (Columbia International eHealth Laboratory) dictionary is the de-facto reference concept dictionary for OpenMRS; most new implementations start from it. It maps concepts to international terminologies including ICD-10, SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm, and CVX.
source: Open Concept Lab — CIEL dictionary
section: Open Concept Lab — CIEL Dictionary

title: Open Concept Lab (OCL)
text: Open Concept Lab (OCL, openconceptlab.org) is a cloud terminology platform that publishes curated subsets of source dictionaries such as CIEL; OpenMRS implementations subscribe to a managed concept collection via the OCL module.
source: Open Concept Lab
section: Open Concept Lab — Terminology Governance

title: OpenMRS information model (obs / encounter / visit)
text: In OpenMRS an Observation (obs) is one piece of information recorded about a patient at a point in time, with a Concept as its 'question' and a typed value (numeric, coded, text, or date). Observations belong to an Encounter (a single patient-provider interaction with a type, datetime, location and provider), and encounters belong to a Visit.
source: OpenMRS Information Model
section: OpenMRS Information Model

title: OpenMRS concept dictionary
text: The OpenMRS concept dictionary defines every question and answer that can be recorded — each concept's name, code, datatype and class. A patient's chart is largely a set of coded observations whose clinical meaning comes from the concept dictionary (commonly CIEL).
source: OpenMRS Wiki — Concept Dictionary Basics
section: OpenMRS Concept Dictionary Basics

title: First-line treatment of uncomplicated malaria
text: For uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, confirm the diagnosis parasitologically (rapid diagnostic test or microscopy) before treating, and use an artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) — for example artemether-lumefantrine — as first-line.
source: WHO Guidelines for malaria
section: WHO Malaria 2025 Section 5.2

title: Severe malaria
text: Severe malaria is a medical emergency: treat with parenteral artesunate for at least 24 hours, then complete a full course of an oral ACT once the patient can tolerate oral therapy.
source: WHO Guidelines for malaria
section: WHO Malaria 2025 Section 5.5

title: Drug-susceptible TB first-line regimen
text: Drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis is treated with a 6-month regimen: 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, then 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin (2HRZE/4HR).
source: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 4: Treatment — drug-susceptible tuberculosis treatment
section: WHO TB Module 4 (2022) Section 3

title: WHO routine infant immunization schedule
text: WHO-recommended routine infant immunization: BCG and hepatitis B at birth; oral polio (OPV) plus pentavalent (DTP-hepatitis B-Hib) at 6, 10 and 14 weeks; a measles-containing vaccine (MCV1) at 9 months and MCV2 at 15-18 months.
source: WHO recommendations for routine immunization — summary tables
section: WHO Routine Immunization Table 2

title: Cryptococcal disease in advanced HIV
text: In advanced HIV disease, screen for cryptococcal antigen (CrAg). Cryptococcal meningitis is treated with antifungal induction (amphotericin B plus flucytosine, or fluconazole where amphotericin is unavailable) followed by consolidation and maintenance fluconazole.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 5.3 — Cryptococcal disease

title: Second-line antiretroviral therapy
text: After confirmed failure of a first-line antiretroviral regimen, switch to second-line: change the nucleoside backbone and use a boosted protease inhibitor or dolutegravir, guided by the treatment history and, where available, resistance testing.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 4.5 — Second-line ART regimens

title: Advanced HIV disease (AHD) diagnostic and prophylaxis package
text: Adults and adolescents presenting with CD4 < 200 cells/mm3 or WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 disease (and all children < 5 years with HIV) meet criteria for advanced HIV disease. WHO recommends delivering an AHD package including rapid ART initiation (unless TB or cryptococcal meningitis is suspected), TB screening plus urine LF-LAM and Xpert MTB/RIF, serum cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) screening at CD4 < 100 cells/mm3 (consider at < 200), co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, and fluconazole pre-emptive therapy for CrAg-positive patients without meningitis.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 5.1 — Package of care for advanced HIV disease

title: HIV viral load monitoring and confirmed virological failure
text: WHO recommends routine HIV viral load testing 6 months after ART initiation, at 12 months, and every 12 months thereafter. Virological failure is defined as two consecutive viral load results > 1000 copies/mL at least 3 months apart with enhanced adherence counselling between tests, triggering a prompt switch to second-line ART.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 4.8 — Monitoring response to ART

title: Oral and oesophageal candidiasis in HIV (WHO Stage 3/4 OI)
text: Persistent oral candidiasis (thrush) in a person with HIV is a WHO stage 3 condition indicating immunosuppression, whereas oesophageal candidiasis (odynophagia or dysphagia) is stage 4. Treat uncomplicated oral candidiasis with topical nystatin suspension or miconazole buccal tablets (or oral fluconazole for moderate-to-severe or refractory disease), and treat oesophageal candidiasis with systemic oral fluconazole for 14–21 days while evaluating ART status and CD4 count.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 3 & Section 5 — Fungal opportunistic infections

title: Efavirenz (EFV) CNS adverse effects and transition to dolutegravir
text: Efavirenz (EFV) frequently causes early neuropsychiatric and central nervous system adverse effects (dizziness, insomnia, abnormal dreams, mood changes) and induces CYP3A4/CYP2B6 metabolism, reducing exposure to co-administered medicines such as lumefantrine, methadone, and azole antifungals. WHO prefers dolutegravir-based regimens (TLD) and supports transitioning patients from EFV-based ART to DTG for better tolerability, fewer drug interactions, and higher barrier to resistance.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 4.3–4.4 — Transition from NNRTIs

title: Nevirapine (NVP) hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity rash, and phase-out
text: Nevirapine (NVP) carries a significant risk of severe, potentially life-threatening hepatotoxicity and cutaneous hypersensitivity (including Stevens-Johnson syndrome), particularly in the first 6–12 weeks or at higher CD4 counts, as well as rapid emergence of NNRTI resistance and CYP3A4 reduction when combined with rifampicin. WHO no longer recommends NVP for adult first-line ART and advises transitioning existing patients to dolutegravir-based regimens.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 4.3 — Phasing out nevirapine

title: Zidovudine (AZT) haematological toxicity and anaemia precautions
text: Zidovudine (AZT, often formulated as AZT/3TC) can cause dose-limiting macrocytic anaemia and neutropenia, especially in advanced HIV disease or baseline haemoglobin < 7–8 g/dL. Monitor haemoglobin at baseline when clinically indicated and on symptoms of pallor or fatigue; substitute tenofovir (TDF) or abacavir (ABC) if severe anaemia or neutropenia develops.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 4.4 — Managing NRTI toxicities

title: Tenofovir (TDF) renal safety and alternative backbones
text: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) is the preferred NRTI backbone in adult ART but can cause proximal renal tubular dysfunction and reduced eGFR, especially with baseline kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, or concurrent nephrotoxic drugs (such as NSAIDs or aminoglycosides). Check serum creatinine or eGFR before or during therapy when risk factors exist and switch to abacavir (ABC) or TAF if renal function declines.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 4.4 — TDF nephrotoxicity monitoring

title: Co-administering rifampicin-based TB treatment (RHZE) with ART
text: Rifampicin potently induces UGT1A1, CYP3A4, and CYP2B6. When treating active TB with rifampicin (RHZE) alongside dolutegravir (DTG), increase dolutegravir dosing to 50 mg twice daily during TB therapy and for 2 weeks after rifampicin ends. Avoid co-administering rifampicin with nevirapine or standard-dose protease inhibitors due to subtherapeutic ARV levels and hepatotoxicity.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 5.4 — Rifampicin-ARV drug interactions

title: Tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) regimens in PLHIV
text: People living with HIV without active TB (negative four-symptom screen: current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats) should receive TB preventive treatment. WHO recommends 3 months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine (3HP — compatible with efavirenz and standard-dose dolutegravir, avoid with protease inhibitors/nevirapine), 1 month daily isoniazid-rifapentine (1HP), or 6–9 months daily isoniazid (6H/9H) with pyridoxine supplementation.
source: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 1: Prevention — tuberculosis preventive treatment
section: WHO TB Module 1 (2024) Section 3 — TPT regimens

title: Febrile illness, tachycardia, and sepsis red-flag assessment in HIV primary care
text: Persistent or acute fever paired with tachycardia, hypotension (systolic BP < 90 mmHg), altered mental status, or advanced HIV requires prompt assessment for severe sepsis, malaria (parasitological RDT/microscopy), tuberculosis, and opportunistic infections. Obtain blood cultures/malaria testing immediately where available, start fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum empiric antibacterials without delay for sepsis danger signs.
source: WHO IMAI District Clinician Manual: Hospital care for adolescents and adults, Vol 1
section: WHO IMAI Volume 1 — Fever and septic shock

title: Persistent and chronic diarrhoea assessment in HIV
text: Persistent or chronic diarrhoea (> 14 days) in a person living with HIV is a WHO clinical stage 3–4 indicator and can rapidly cause dehydration, electrolyte loss, and malabsorption of antiretroviral medicines. Assess hydration, start oral rehydration solution (ORS), evaluate for bacterial dysentery, Cryptosporidium, or Clostridioides difficile, and review ART adherence/regimen tolerance.
source: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring
section: WHO HIV 2021 Section 3 & Section 5 — Chronic diarrhoea

title: Malaria ACT selection and antimalarial-ARV interactions
text: When treating uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in patients receiving CYP3A4/CYP2B6-inducing antiretroviral medicines such as efavirenz or nevirapine (or rifampicin), plasma exposure to artemether and lumefantrine drops substantially, raising risk of recrudescence; counsel on fat-containing food intake and monitor closely for clinical/parasitological response. Avoid artesunate-amodiaquine with zidovudine (risk of severe neutropenia) or efavirenz (hepatotoxicity risk).
source: WHO Guidelines for malaria
section: WHO Malaria 2025 Section 5.2 & Co-administration with ARVs

title: Acute upper respiratory infection (coryza) antibiotic stewardship
text: Uncomplicated acute upper respiratory tract infections (acute coryza, common cold, non-purulent rhinitis) are predominantly viral and self-limiting. Under WHO AWaRe primary care guidance, do not prescribe antibiotics for acute viral URI; offer symptomatic relief (fluids, paracetamol/antipyretics) and red-flag return precautions.
source: The WHO AWaRe (Access, Watch, Reserve) antibiotic book
section: WHO AWaRe Antibiotic Book — Acute upper respiratory infections

title: Arthritis pain relief and NSAID nephrotoxicity precautions
text: For joint pain or osteoarthritis, start with non-pharmacological measures, physical activity, topical NSAIDs, or oral paracetamol when appropriate. If an oral NSAID (such as ibuprofen) is required, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration and avoid chronic systemic NSAIDs in patients with renal impairment, dehydration, heart failure, active peptic ulcer disease, or concurrent tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF).
source: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, 23rd list
section: WHO EML Section 2 — Non-opioids and NSAIDs

title: Hypertension, diabetes, and dolutegravir-metformin dose limit
text: In adults with hypertension and type 2 diabetes (including people living with HIV), target blood pressure < 140/90 mmHg (or < 130/80 mmHg in higher cardiovascular risk), monitor serum creatinine/eGFR, and avoid drug-induced nephrotoxicity. Importantly, dolutegravir inhibits OCT2 and MATE1 renal transporters and nearly doubles metformin exposure: limit metformin to a maximum of 1000 mg/day when co-administered with dolutegravir and monitor tolerability/renal function.
source: WHO Package of Essential Noncommunicable (PEN) Disease Interventions & WHO HIV 2021
section: WHO PEN & WHO HIV 2021 Section 5.8 — Noncommunicable diseases & ARV interactions
